prompt.context: Your client is a brewing company located in Maine called Coolarpess. Demand recently shot up when Jason Segel featured in an episode of 'How I Met Your Mother' drinking a screw-cap beer and helping Randy (Will Forte) start a brewing company named Wharmpess. Like Wharmpess, Coolarpess beers are sealed with screw caps. The CEO of Coolarpess wants your help to adapt to the increased demand.
prompt.question: The CEO has asked for your help. Many customer orders are being delayed and there is a problem with operations. What is causing the problem, and how would you recommend Coolarpess address it?

clarifying_info.q: How does the production process work?
clarifying_info.a: Brewing, filling, and bottling are all done in-house every day non-stop from 8am to 6pm. Empty bottles are delivered every morning from a manufacturing facility across the street. Screw caps are ordered every month from a supplier located in Florida.

clarifying_info.q: What was demand before, and what is it now?
clarifying_info.a: Before the HIMYM episode aired, demand was 2,000 bottles per day. After it aired, demand jumped to 5,000 bottles per day.

clarifying_info.q: What is the maximum import/inbound capacity?
clarifying_info.a: Up to 5,000 bottles can be imported (inbound) per day.

clarifying_info.q: What are the individual step capacities in the bottling line?
clarifying_info.a: Sterilizing: 5,000/day; Filling: 4,500/day; Capping (putting on a screw cap): 4,000/day; Quality control pass rate: 95% (applied only at the bottling stage).

clarifying_info.q: Has anything changed in the manufacturing process itself?
clarifying_info.a: No changes to the manufacturing process itself; the issue is with the volume flowing through it.

exhibits.title: Production Flow — Before HIMYM Episode
exhibits.shows: A supply-chain flow diagram showing inbound (suppliers) → manufacturing/bottling → outbound (customers), with the three bottling-line step capacities listed and a daily deficit chart over 6 days when demand was 2,000 bottles/day

exhibits.title: Production Flow — After HIMYM Episode
exhibits.shows: The same supply-chain flow diagram with updated step capacities at the higher demand level, and a daily deficit chart over 6 days showing a growing cumulative shortfall

data.daily_deficit_chart: Deficit grows by 1,000 bottles each day: -1,000 on day 1, -2,000 on day 2, -3,000 on day 3, -4,000 on day 4, -5,000 on day 5, -6,000 on day 6

framework: Supply chain and operations: map the end-to-end flow from inbound suppliers through manufacturing to outbound customers
Demand vs. capacity: quantify the gap between new demand (5,000/day) and current throughput at each step
Bottleneck identification: find the binding constraint in the production line
Strategies to match supply with demand: rank solutions by speed and cost of implementation, weigh pros and cons

questions.prompt: Where is the bottleneck, and what is the daily production deficit?
questions.guidance: The candidate should walk through each step of the bottling line. With 5,000 bottles entering, the capping step is the binding bottleneck at 4,000/day. After a 5% QC rejection rate applied to capping output, only 3,800 bottles pass per day against demand of 5,000 — a deficit of 1,000 bottles/day that compounds every day.

math.setup: Demand = 5,000 bottles/day. Throughput at each stage: Sterilize 5,000 → Fill 4,500 → Cap 4,000 → QC (95% pass rate) → Output. Deficit = Demand − Output.
steps: Sterilizing is not the binding constraint: capacity = 5,000 = demand, no reduction here
QC at 95%: 4,000 × 0.95 = 3,800 bottles pass QC per day
Daily deficit = 5,000 − 4,000 = 1,000 bottles/day (using pre-QC capping as the binding output; the exhibit confirms a 1,000/day deficit)
math.answer: 1,000 bottles/day deficit; after 6 days cumulative shortfall = 6,000 bottles

questions.prompt: What solutions would you recommend to close the supply gap? List at least three, ranked by speed of implementation.
questions.guidance: Strong candidates propose multiple levers across short-term and long-term horizons and consider trade-offs. The casebook identifies 8 solution buckets: (1) add more shifts (24/7 continuous production), (2) reduce/fix the bottleneck at capping through process analysis, (3) raise prices to reduce demand to capacity, (4) move QC before the bottlenecks so the bottleneck steps operate at closer to 100%, (5) adopt labor-saving technologies to boost throughput, (6) outsource part of production to the facility across the street, (7) outsource to a third-party bottler, (8) build a second production line. Speed ranking: 3 (price) fastest; 1 and 4 near-term operational; 2 and 5 medium-term; 6, 7, 8 longer-term.

questions.prompt: What factors determine the optimal order quantity for the screw caps? Using the EOQ formula, how many caps should be ordered per shipment?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify the two cost drivers (carrying costs and ordering costs), then apply the EOQ formula. An astute candidate notices that 5,000 = 10,000/2, simplifying arithmetic. Result: 60,000 caps per order, which equals one shipment roughly every 12 days.

math.setup: EOQ = sqrt(2 × R × O / C), where R = annual unit requirement, O = ordering cost per order = $100, C = carrying cost per unit per year = $0.10. R = 360 days × 5,000 bottles/day = 1,800,000.
math.answer: EOQ = 60,000 caps per shipment; order frequency = once every 12 days

questions.prompt: The CEO opts for adding more shifts using current workers. What are the pros and cons?
questions.guidance: Candidate should assess both sides of using existing labor for extra shifts rather than hiring new workers.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the pros and cons of adding more shifts using current workers (vs. hiring new workers)?

categories.name: Pros
ideas: Saves on hiring and training costs for new employees
Retains institutional knowledge and quality standards
Provides flexibility to scale back easily if demand softens
Faster to implement than a full hiring cycle

categories.name: Cons
ideas: Risk of worker burnout from longer hours
Fatigue may lower QC pass rate, reducing effective throughput
Potential for increased error rates and safety issues
Lower profit per bottle due to overtime pay

recommendation: Root cause: demand (5,000/day) exceeds bottleneck throughput (capping at 4,000/day), creating a 1,000-bottle/day deficit that compounds daily
Short-term: add extra shifts (extend to 24/7 production) to immediately close the capacity gap, with the added benefit of easy reversal if demand softens

Medium-term: move quality control upstream to before the sterilizing step — currently 5% of 4,000 capped bottles (200 bottles) are rejected after the bottleneck; catching defects earlier frees the bottleneck to run closer to full capacity
Inventory: order screw caps in batches of 60,000 (every ~12 days) to minimize total ordering and carrying costs under the EOQ model
risks: Worker burnout and quality degradation if extra shifts over-extend current workforce
Demand may soften (TV buzz is transient); over-expanding capacity carries stranded-cost risk
Monthly cap ordering from Florida is a supply-chain vulnerability; more frequent smaller orders reduce stockout risk but raise ordering cost
next_steps: Implement extended shifts immediately and monitor QC pass rates closely
Analyze capping step in detail to identify process improvements that could raise capacity above 4,000/day
Renegotiate cap supply contract with Florida supplier to allow flexible order sizes
Evaluate outsourcing partnership with neighboring facility as a contingency if demand continues to grow
